extracted.intended_audience: academic economists and empirical researchers studying education, religion, and development (graduate students, referees, replication researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reporting standards for an empirical economics paper studying the impact of mass public schooling and Islamic school entry, including econometric specifications (OLS/IV), instruments and diagnostics, fixed effects and clustering choices, variable construction, and a formal theoretical model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and comparison of OLS and IV specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate baseline specifications by OLS and, where endogeneity is a concern, by IV. Compare OLS and IV estimates and test whether they are identical (e.g., Hausman GMM test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both OLS and IV results in tables (odd-numbered columns OLS, even-numbered IV in this paper). Use Hausman GMM to test equality; if Hausman rejects (p-value<0.01) interpret IV as addressing endogeneity and consider LATE interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument selection and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrument for endogenous regressors (e.g., Islamic elementary school entry) using plausible exogenous mobilization mechanisms such as waqf endowment base, potential rice yields, and Muslim population share (and their interactions with exposure/cohort indicators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how instruments capture supply shifts (resource availability) and why they plausibly affect the endogenous regressors but not outcomes directly. Expand instrument sets with higher-order interactions where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-stage strength diagnostics
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that instruments are collectively strong using first-stage statistics such as the KP first-stage Wald statistic (cluster-robust F) and the Kleibergen and Paap multivariate Wald analogue, and Sanderson and Windmeijer tests on separate first stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report KP/Wald statistics and p-values; reject weak instruments null (e.g., p-values<0.01) and report relevant multivariate analogues when using multiple endogenous regressors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underidentification and weak-IV testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Report tests that the system is identified (e.g., KP 1st stage LM test of the null of underidentification) and additional weak-instrument diagnostics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide LM test p-values for underidentification and any additional diagnostics (e.g., Sanderson-Windmeijer) demonstrating adequate first-stage strength for each endogenous regressor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust standard errors and clustering
rubrics_metrics.description: Use robust standard errors clustered at an appropriate level (in this paper: clustered by district or district of birth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clustering level explicitly in table notes (e.g., 'Robust standard errors clustered by district of birth'). Use cluster-robust statistics for first-stage KP F when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed effects specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Include high-dimensional fixed effects appropriate to the design: e.g., district × survey-year FE, cohort FE, cohort FE interacted with baseline district characteristics (1957 Islamic Schools × Cohort FE), and other relevant FE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify which fixed effects are included in each column; when interacting instruments or treatment with cohort indicators, include corresponding interacted FE to absorb confounding trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization and variable construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct key treatment variables as normalized counts (e.g., 'Islamic elementary equals the total new Islamic school constructions during 1973–78 normalized by the district’s child population in 1971'; SD INPRES entry similarly normalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly report how variables are measured and normalized (denominator year and population definition). This is essential for interpretation and replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction terms to capture heterogeneous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use interaction terms to capture heterogeneous exposure effects (e.g., INPRES × young interacted with standardized vote share of Islamic parties in 1950s elections; triple interactions with cohort FE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe and report interactions explicitly; when interacting treatments with baseline district characteristics, include corresponding interacted fixed effects and interpret interaction coefficients (e.g., negative interaction implies substitution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting sample sizes and summary statistics in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables should report number of individuals (observations), number of districts, the dependent variable mean, and R-squared for each specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these quantities underneath coefficient blocks as done in the appendix tables: 'Number of Individuals', 'Number of Districts', 'Dep. Var. Mean', and 'R2'. This aids interpretation of magnitude and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance notation and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard significance stars and thresholds: * p<0.1, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01. Interpret effect sizes at sample means where helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the significance-key note in table captions/notes and use it consistently across tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and alternative specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Augment baseline DID/specifications with alternative regressors, add additional controls and interactions, and run OLS and IV variants to assess robustness (e.g., allow Islamic primary entry alongside SD INPRES entry and interact with exposed cohorts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how adding controls or alternative measures affects point estimates and standard errors; explain discrepancies (e.g., IV larger than OLS) and possible interpretations (LATE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of IV estimates as LATE
rubrics_metrics.description: When IV estimates differ substantially from OLS (e.g., IV significantly larger; p-value<0.01 for difference), interpret IV as estimating a local average treatment effect for compliers induced by the instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain what the instruments plausibly shift (e.g., supply-side entry) and which subpopulations are compliers whose behavior is captured by IV estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of dependent variables and conditional regressions
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing outcomes across institution types, condition on total years-of-schooling fixed effects to identify differential outcomes for given schooling quantity (e.g., regress literacy indicators on Islamic vs non-Islamic school indicators conditional on years-of-schooling FE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the conditional variable explicitly and explain the interpretation (differential literacy holding total schooling constant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple data sources and sample restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine and report results across data sources (e.g., 2010 Population Census, Susenas 2012–18, Pepinsky et al. 2018 survey), and impose consistent sample restrictions (e.g., restrict to cohorts born 1957–1987 and exclude partially exposed cohorts 1963–67 where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe why particular samples or cohort windows are used and report results separately by data source and subgroup (Muslims vs Non-Muslims; Islamic-educated vs Secular-educated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and interpretation of substitution/complementarity tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Augment regression with both types of school entry and their interaction; interpret a negative interaction term as evidence that the two types of schools are substitutes (i.e., counteracting effects when both enter simultaneously).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate OLS and IV versions; compute implied marginal effects at sample means (e.g., effect of each school on years of education if each enters alone and the reduction when both enter jointly).

rubrics_metrics.name: District-level regression design and geographic controls
rubrics_metrics.description: For district-level outcomes (e.g., electoral measures), include province fixed effects and use district-level regressions where the dependent variable can be binary indicators for exceedance thresholds (e.g., whether Golkar vote share is >1 or >1.5 SDs above mean).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report dependent variable mean, number of districts, and R2. Use appropriate fixed effects to control for large-scale regional confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical reporting with regression-based country-specific estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: When plotting cross-country correlations (e.g., education and religiosity in World Values Survey), compute country-specific regression estimates pooling across waves, controlling for age, gender, religious denomination and survey-year fixed effects, and report point estimates with 95% CIs based on robust standard errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State how the outcome and key independent variables are defined (e.g., education = indicator for high school completion; religiosity = binary 'religious' response) and explicitly list control variables used in each regression underlying plotted points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit notes in table captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide detailed table notes describing the regression equation used, variable definitions, instruments, fixed effects, sample, and interpretation of reported statistics (e.g., what KP statistics represent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use table notes to document specification parity across columns and to explain any deviations from baseline specifications; clarify which columns are OLS/IV and which instruments are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical model primitives and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting a stylized model, state primitives and assumptions: N markets, unit mass of students per market, preferences uniformly distributed over [0,J], student utility ui(k)=vk − (xk − ρi)^2, state schools set xs=0, religious schools choose xr>0, state quality vs and religious quality vr with vr < vs < 2vr, fixed entry cost =1, state budget S < N, religious budget R=αS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List timing of moves, clarify parameter ranges (e.g., J > 2√vr in the paper), and justify qualitative assumptions with empirical evidence when possible (e.g., test-score differentials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model timing and solution by backward induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify game timing explicitly: (1) state decides market entry; (2) religious sector decides entry; (3) religious schools set curricula; (4) students choose schools. Solve model by backward induction and characterize equilibria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staged solution to derive equilibrium curricula, entry patterns (major/minor markets), and comparative statics for budget windfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and characterization of market types (major/minor) and equilibrium conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define major markets (e.g., satisfying J ≥ 2 vs) and minor markets, characterize when schools can coexist without active competition, and state equilibrium conditions depending on budgets (e.g., if S + R ≤ N + m no minor market competition; if S + R > N + m both enter major markets and the largest minor markets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide constructive examples and lemmas that rule out certain allocations (e.g., Lemmas showing deviations to larger markets), and explain multiplicity of equilibria arising from how smaller markets are split.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model implications for empirical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive testable implications: mass public schooling increases markets with both types of schools; higher α (religious sector fundraising capacity) increases religious entry; state entry induces religious curriculum differentiation to be more religious; religious secondary education increases co-location with public schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these implications to motivate empirical specifications, choice of outcomes (entry, curriculum measures, literacy, ideology), and interpretation of heterogeneous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of weak-IV and underidentification tests in multi-instrument/multi-endogenous settings
rubrics_metrics.description: When instrumenting multiple endogenous variables (e.g., interacting instruments with INPRES and cohort indicators), use multivariate analogues of first-stage F-statistics (Kleibergen-Paap) and report separate-first-stage tests (Sanderson and Windmeijer) to reject weak instruments null.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state which multivariate diagnostics are reported and ensure separate-first-stage strength for each endogenous variable; include LM tests for underidentification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and presentation of substitution magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify substitution/complementarity by calculating effect sizes at sample means (e.g., own effect of each school ~0.35 years of education when entering alone, reduced by 0.25 years when both enter jointly) and discuss how competition biases baseline estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate interaction coefficient estimates into intuitive units (years of schooling) at observed means of regressors and discuss policy-relevant magnitudes and biases.
